\title{{\bf Mergeability Has a History}}
\subtitle{Training provenance determines removable representation mismatch}
\author{\textbf{Suchir Salhan} \\ sas245@cam.ac.uk}
\institute[CL]{Computer Laboratory, University of Cambridge, UK}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}

\begin{frame}
  \titlepage
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The arc}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item \structure{How similar are two trained models?} Layer-wise and pairwise CKA across
          languages, scales and families; Procrustes alignment, reconstruction and causal patching.
    \item \structure{Can they be combined?} Merging fails for two different reasons and the
          field's tooling does not distinguish them --- two models can be incompatible because
          they organise the same computation under \emph{different coordinates}, or because they
          \emph{learned different things}. The first is removable by a function-preserving map;
          the second is not.
  \end{enumerate}
  \vfill
  \begin{block}{The result in one line}
    \alert{Training provenance decides which one you have} --- not how different two runs were,
    but whether they were \alert{initialised together}. That obstruction is fixed at step 0:
    drift is exactly zero, so training neither creates nor removes it.
  \end{block}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{From similarity to composability}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item So far: how much structure two models \structure{share}, measured with CKA, Procrustes
          alignment, patching and reconstruction.
    \item High similarity does not imply the models can be \structure{combined} --- averaging two
          networks that compute the same thing in different coordinates destroys the computation.
    \item The rest of the deck asks the composability question directly, and treats alignment as
          an \alert{intervention} rather than as a correlate.
  \end{itemize}
  \vfill
  \begin{block}{The question}
    When can representational alignment rescue model merging, and when can it not?
  \end{block}
\end{frame}

\section{Parameter distance is not functional distance}

\begin{frame}[plain,noframenumbering]
  \vfill
  \begin{center}
    {\usebeamercolor[fg]{structure}\Large\bfseries Parameter distance is not functional distance}
  \end{center}
  \vfill
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{A permutation moves the weights as far as possible and changes nothing}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.68\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig23_invariance.pdf}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{-0.3em}{\footnotesize Four transformations of one checkpoint. The valid permutations are exact to round-off; a random orthogonal moves the weights the same distance and breaks the function 29,000$\times$ more.}
\end{frame}

\section{Provenance determines the cost of composing}

\begin{frame}[plain,noframenumbering]
  \vfill
  \begin{center}
    {\usebeamercolor[fg]{structure}\Large\bfseries Provenance determines the cost of composing}
  \end{center}
  \vfill
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Initialisation costs four times what data order costs, and only the first is removable}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.68\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig21_provenance_ladder.pdf}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{-0.3em}{\footnotesize A fitted map removes 93\% of the initialisation gap and makes the data-order gap \emph{worse} by 27\%. The curriculum rung splits by whether the pair shares an initialisation --- a split recovered from the weights, not the training logs.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{The gap is there at every depth, not at one seam}
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.68\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig20_stitch_curves.pdf}
  \end{center}
  \vspace{-0.3em}{\footnotesize Stitch penalty as a function of where the two models are joined.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{What to take away}
  \begin{itemize}
    \item Alignment does not make models mergeable. It removes \structure{one} obstruction, and
          that obstruction is present when, and essentially only when, two models were
          \structure{initialised apart}.
    \item Data order, curriculum and even first language leave models in a shared coordinate
          system if they started from the same weights.
    \item Distance does not explain the rescue; arbitrary maps do not; flexibility does not.
          \alert{Group membership does.}
    \item The coordinate share never decays: two runs differing only in initialisation grow
          $916\times$ more expensive to compose while the removable fraction stays above 92\%.
  \end{itemize}
  \vfill
  \begin{block}{}
    Whatever pretraining does to make two models incompatible, it is not making their difference
    irreducible.
  \end{block}
\end{frame}
